stages.title: Advanced fine-art composition
stages.hook: How might a painter predict where a viewer's eye will travel, and does the path change with the viewer's purpose?
explain: Composition at an advanced level is the management of attention, tension and meaning. Gestalt principles describe how viewers group elements automatically: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and figure-ground. Rudolf Arnheim, in Art and Visual Perception (1954), applied this to art, arguing that visual forces such as balance, weight and direction act on every element in a field.

Visual hierarchy ranks what is seen first, second and third using contrast, scale, isolation, edge sharpness and colour intensity. Pictorial space can be deep, shallow or deliberately flat. Alfred Yarbus reported in 1967 that eye movements vary with the viewer's task, though later replications give mixed support, so predictions of gaze remain probabilistic. Different traditions organise space differently: Chinese hand scrolls unroll in time, Persian miniatures use multiple viewpoints and ornamental borders, and Mesoamerican codices use register and glyph sequence.

Proportion systems are tools. Root-two rectangles, such as the ISO A-series paper with sides in ratio 1 to √2 (about 1.414), keep their proportion when halved. Critics note that claims about universal proportion in masterpieces are often weak. A sound composition analysis states the visual evidence, the hypothesised effect, and the alternatives it considered.

example.q: A sheet of A4 paper measures 210 mm by 297 mm. What is the ratio of long side to short side, to three decimals, and what does it show?
steps: So the sheet approximates the root-two ratio, which is preserved when halved.

stages.title: Professional painting techniques
stages.hook: What would you need to know about a tube of paint to be sure a painting made with it will last a century?
explain: Professional practice begins with materials. A paint is pigment suspended in a binder: drying oil for oil paint, acrylic polymer emulsion for acrylic, gum arabic for watercolour, egg yolk for tempera. Pigments differ in opacity, tinting strength, toxicity and permanence. Examples: lead white is warm and dense but toxic, titanium white is bright and opaque, Prussian blue was first made in the early 1700s, and synthetic ultramarine was commercialised in 1826, replacing costly lapis lazuli.

Supports and grounds determine stability. Canvas is stretched on a frame and sized to protect it from the acid of oil; gesso grounds give tooth. Panels need stable wood and bracing. The lightfastness rating on a tube (for example ASTM I or II) predicts fading resistance. Professionals keep records of materials, protect finished works with removable varnish, and practise safe handling of solvents, dust and heavy-metal pigments such as cadmium and lead.

Techniques differ by tradition: egg tempera on panel, buon fresco in wet plaster, oil glazing in Northern Europe, ink-and-colour on silk in East Asia, natural earth pigments on bark and canvas in Indigenous Australia. A professional can explain why a technique was chosen, not only how to perform it.

example.q: A canvas is 60 cm by 80 cm. A stretcher is square when its two diagonals are equal. What should each diagonal measure?

stages.title: Advanced three-dimensional artistic design
stages.hook: What does it mean for a three-dimensional object to be well designed, and who decides?
explain: Three-dimensional design joins form, function, material and context. Louis Sullivan wrote in 1896 that "form ever follows function" in the context of tall office buildings, and the slogan became a modernist principle. The Bauhaus, founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919, taught design as a combination of art, craft and industry. Critics later argued that function alone does not decide form, because culture, symbolism and pleasure also matter.

Design process moves from research and sketches to models and prototypes, with testing and revision. Ergonomics tests fit to the human body. Material selection weighs strength, weight, cost, finish, sustainability and the energy to make and recycle. Joints (dovetail, mortise and tenon, welding, bolts) transfer loads. Tolerance is the allowable variation in a dimension. Modular design uses repeated units that fit together.

Global design traditions offer many models: Japanese joinery that uses wood joints without nails, West African stools carved from single logs, Scandinavian furniture of simple forms, and Isamu Noguchi's sculptural furniture. Design ethics include accessibility, repairability and the life cycle of materials.

example.q: A solid cube has sides 40 cm. A hollow version has walls 2 cm thick on all sides. How many cm³ of material does the hollow cube use?

stages.title: Contemporary artistic movements
stages.hook: Since the 1950s art has asked "what counts as art?" again and again. Which answers seem most convincing to you, and why?
explain: After modernism, art became more varied. Pop art in Britain and the United States in the 1950s and 1960s took imagery from advertising and mass culture: Richard Hamilton's collage of 1956 and Andy Warhol's soup can paintings of 1962. Minimalism in the 1960s, with Donald Judd and Dan Flavin, reduced work to simple industrial forms. Conceptual and performance art put ideas and actions first: Yoko Ono's Cut Piece (1964) invited the audience to take part.

Feminist art challenged exclusion. Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party (1974 to 1979) honoured women of history. Postmodernism questioned grand narratives and mixed styles. Neo-expressionism in the 1980s included Jean-Michel Basquiat. Street art and muralism moved art into public space. The 1989 exhibition Magiciens de la Terre in Paris is often cited as a turning point in showing living artists from across the world together, though critics have debated its framing.

Contemporary art is now global, with major centres and biennials in Dakar, Havana, Sharjah, São Paulo, Johannesburg, Venice and many more. Themes include identity, migration, ecology, memory and technology. Critics ask who gets shown, who writes the history, and how markets shape taste.

stages.title: Art conservation and materials
stages.hook: What would you do first to find out whether a painting is original, damaged or restored?
explain: Conservation protects cultural heritage. Preventive conservation controls the environment: stable temperature, relative humidity often kept around 45 to 55%, controlled light (UV is filtered), pest management, clean storage and careful handling. Interventive conservation treats objects, guided by principles: minimal intervention, reversibility where possible, compatible materials and full documentation.

Causes of deterioration include light fading, humidity swings that crack paint on wood or canvas, acid in paper, pests, pollutants, and past restorations. Technical examination reveals more than the eye: X-radiography shows lead-containing underlayers and changes, infrared reflectography reveals underdrawing, X-ray fluorescence identifies elements in pigments, and dendrochronology dates wood panels by tree rings. Radiocarbon dating dates organic material, with a carbon-14 half-life of about 5,730 years.

Ethics are debated. Cleaning of the Sistine Chapel ceiling from 1980 to 1994 revealed brighter colours and sparked disagreement. A 2012 amateur attempt to retouch the Ecce Homo fresco in Borja, Spain, caused widespread concern. Conservation also respects living traditions, for instance where sacred objects are renewed by communities rather than preserved unchanged.

example.q: A sample has 25% of its original carbon-14. About how old is it? (half-life 5,730 years)
steps: Check: older than one half-life but younger than three.

analogies.home: Keeping photos out of sunlight and damp is preventive conservation.
analogies.farm: Seed stores are dry and cool to prevent mould, like archives.
analogies.city: Museums use air control like a building's climate system.
analogies.nature: Natural pigments in leaves fade in sun, showing why light matters.

stages.title: Advanced digital art
stages.hook: If a computer can generate an image, who is the author, and what skills still matter?
explain: Advanced digital practice rests on technical understanding. Colour management uses ICC profiles to keep colour consistent between devices, and common screen standards such as sRGB define the colour range. Bit depth sets how many levels each channel has: 8 bits per channel gives 256 levels, and three channels give 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 colours. Higher bit depth reduces banding in gradients.

Workflows may be non-destructive, using layers, masks, adjustment layers and smart objects. Procedural and generative art uses rules or algorithms, sometimes with randomness. Photogrammetry builds 3D models from many photographs. Real-time engines render interactive scenes. Accessibility practice includes text descriptions and sufficient contrast.

AI image generators raise contested questions about authorship, consent, copyright and labour, since many are trained on large collections of existing images. Laws and norms differ between countries and are changing, so artists keep records of their process and check licences. Digital art builds on traditional skills, and artists in places from Lagos to Seoul work in these media.

example.q: An uncompressed 1920 × 1080 image has 3 channels at 8 bits each. How many bytes is it?

stages.title: Installation and public art
stages.hook: Who should decide what art stands in a shared public square: artists, officials or residents?
explain: Installation art creates an immersive environment, and the viewer's movement through it is part of the work. Site-specific works are made for one place and respond to its architecture, history and community. Land art and environmental art work with landscape. Public art is accessible to everyone, in streets, parks or transport hubs, and must consider safety, maintenance and consent.

Examples show debates. Richard Serra's Tilted Arc was installed in a New York plaza in 1981 and removed in 1989 after hearings, raising the question of whether a site-specific work can be moved. Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the Reichstag in Berlin in 1995 and installed The Gates in Central Park in 2005. Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate in Chicago was made from 2004 to 2006. Ai Weiwei's Sunflower Seeds filled Tate Modern's Turbine Hall in 2010. Mexican muralists Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painted public murals from the 1920s.

Process matters as much as outcome: consultation with residents, permits, engineering, insurance, fabrication, installation and long-term maintenance. Some cities use percent-for-art policies that set aside a share of construction budgets for art. Public art can be temporary, such as festivals and projections, or permanent. It can celebrate, commemorate, challenge or heal, and communities may disagree about monuments, so decisions about removal or recontextualisation are contested.

stages.title: Cross-cultural artistic investigation
stages.hook: How can you study the art of a culture that is not your own without distorting it?
explain: Cross-cultural investigation compares art across cultures with attention to method and ethics. Good practice includes using primary sources (objects, documents, artists' own words), learning key terms in the original language, acknowledging your own position (positionality), consulting communities, and avoiding projecting your categories onto others. Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) criticised how Western scholarship constructed the East as exotic and unchanging.

Case studies show complexity. Japonisme in the later 1800s transformed European art through admiration but also stereotyping. Picasso and others engaged with African sculpture early in the 1900s, often without crediting makers. Aboriginal artists have campaigned against fake art that imitates Indigenous designs. In the United States, the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (1990) set procedures for returning certain remains and objects to tribes. Debates about appropriation and appreciation depend on power, credit, consent and benefit.

A strong investigation states a clear question, defines terms, selects comparable cases, gathers varied evidence, and tests alternative explanations. It reports limits honestly and shares findings with the communities involved when possible. Collaborative projects that centre community voices, such as co-curated exhibitions, are increasingly common.

example.q: A study of 40 sources finds 28 are by authors from one region. What percentage is that?
steps: Interpret: heavy dependence on one region.

stages.title: Original artistic portfolio and exhibition project
stages.hook: If you had to show who you are as an artist in twelve works and one page of text, what would you include?
explain: A portfolio is a curated body of work that shows a coherent direction, skill and growth. It includes finished works, selected process materials (sketches, tests, maquettes), an artist statement and good documentation. The strongest portfolios have a clear question or theme developed across several pieces, not a random assortment.

The project plan has stages: research and proposal, experimentation, production, critique and revision, documentation, and presentation. Regular critiques with peers test whether intention matches effect. Good documentation uses even light, a neutral background, a scale reference, and sharp, colour-accurate images. An artist statement states what the work explores and how, in plain language without jargon.

Exhibition planning uses a timeline, a budget, a floor plan, a risk assessment, a label plan and accessibility measures. Ethical practice credits sources, obtains permission for images or community material, and acknowledges collaborators. Evaluation compares outcomes with aims: audience response, learning and what to do next. Artists around the world also build practice by joining collectives, residencies and community workshops.

example.q: A budget has materials 300, framing 180, printing 120 and venue costs 400. Funding is 900. What is left or short?
